sources.title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
sources.note: Local machine transcript (faster-whisper), no speaker labels; carded Dex's statements only. Inventory line 157 lists it via a third-party podwise summary.

sources.title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
sources.note: Local machine transcript (faster-whisper), no speaker labels; Dex co-hosts with Vaibhav Gupta; attributed by content. Inventory check for this exact episode found no matching entry in my grep.

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: RPI's not enough. We actually need six steps.
cards.claim: Dex changes his earlier position: research-plan-implement (three steps) was insufficient, and in mid-December 2025 his team moved to a six-step workflow, while still saying the exact prompts and step count are not the point.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on rolling out RPI to customers; team results varied widely; no numbers
cards.landing: Phase routine: do not treat the number of phases as fixed; split planning into more steps if results vary across people

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: people pick up these prompts... their team would have a vast spectrum of quality of results
cards.claim: A prompt set that gives one person excellent results (after about a thousand hours) gives a team a wide spread of quality, so he rebuilt the product around guided workflows instead of asking people to wield six prompts.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed across customer rollouts; no numbers
cards.landing: Workflow library / skills: encode the routine as guided steps rather than prose the agent must remember

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: use control flow for control flow because it's going to be much more reliable.
cards.claim: The create-plan prompt had about 50 instructions; he now splits planning into multiple steps wrapped in deterministic code, applying 12-factor-agents advice not to use prompts for control flow.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as design principle; one prompt of about 50 instructions cited
cards.landing: Phase routine compliance: move ordering from prose into scripts or hooks; split long multi-instruction prompts

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the magic is not in the prompts. There is no perfect prompt.
cards.claim: The durable skill is context engineering and intentional compaction; the specific prompts, and even the number of steps, will change (a bitter-lesson stance).
cards.landing: Treat skill and prompt text as disposable; invest in context discipline

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the more context you use, the worst results you'll get
cards.claim: Smart zone versus dumb zone: output quality falls as context fills, because attention cost grows quadratically with tokens (per layer and per head), so work should stay in the early part of the window.
cards.landing: Context budget: one phase per new session; CLAUDE.md, tools and MCPs consume smart-zone room

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I always say like 40% contact usage
cards.claim: His rule of thumb puts the smart-zone limit at roughly 40% context usage, but he says the exact number does not matter, varies by task type, and that his token count differs from Claude Code's because it includes the autocompact buffer.
cards.landing: Compare with harness plan to consider auto-compaction only past 500k tokens; a 40% line is far lower

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: should this be a new user message or should this be a new context window?
cards.claim: Before every message, ask whether it should be a new context window instead; sometimes keep the old one because re-reading files is slow or a summary cannot be trusted.
cards.landing: One phase per new chat; explicit keep-vs-fresh test in the closing message

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: needle in a haystack is not useful because most of the time you don't need
cards.claim: Needle-in-a-haystack long-context benchmarks mislead because real work needs acting on all the information, or teasing out the relevant 50,000 words, which models are worse at.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributes the point to Geoff Huntley; no benchmark numbers
cards.landing: Do not trust advertised long-context windows as proof that large contexts are safe

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the context window is much longer. The cup is smaller than you think it is
cards.claim: The available smart-zone room is smaller than people think, because system prompt, built-in tools, custom MCPs and CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md all sit in context before the task; levers are tighter specs, cheaper source traversal, fewer MCPs and fewer built-in tools.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: its 390 always-loaded lines spend smart-zone budget

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: custom MCPs is no longer as much of a problem
cards.claim: Change of position on tools: with the tool-search feature, large custom MCP sets are less of a context problem than before, though he had not tried it himself.
cards.landing: MCP/tool loading policy

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: give people visibility and metrics into how much of the context is being used
cards.claim: A Ralph tool should chart context used per iteration and per component so you see that loops always reach 60% and shrink the task; he and Matt note observability here is currently poor.
cards.landing: Measurement of context use per phase (a skipped measurement pipeline in the review)

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Ralph is a system that optimizes for always working in the early part
cards.claim: Ralph is framed as a Kubernetes-style control loop: read specs (desired state) and source (current state), implement one thing, repeat, so every iteration starts in the smart zone.
cards.landing: Fresh-context-per-task loop pattern for long work

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: make the changes, run the test, fix any issues, run the test
cards.claim: Size a task so edit, test, fix, retest and commit all fit in as little context as possible, but not so small that a signature change cannot pass tests without touching other files.
cards.landing: Plan task sizing in the phase routine

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the way I count tokens... they include the end buffer in their percentage
cards.claim: Context percentages are not comparable across tools: Claude Code's displayed percentage includes the reserved autocompact buffer, so thresholds must be stated with the counting method.
cards.landing: Any context-threshold rule in the harness should name how tokens are counted

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the desired state of the world was all the code adheres to the style guide.
cards.claim: Worked Ralph example: a 30-minute Claude interview plus 30 minutes with a front-end engineer produced about 25-27 React style rules, then a Ralph loop on a cloud VM refactored toward them for about six hours.
cards.evidence_detail: About 6 hours, 20 commits, about 20,000-line PR (some plan files); 10 minutes to set up and 10 to tear down the VM
cards.landing: Style guide as the desired-state spec for an overnight refactor loop

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do not send your coworkers 20,000 line PR that refactors the entire code base
cards.claim: The six-hour Ralph PR was never merged (a hundred merge conflicts two days later); his advice is not to send huge autonomous PRs, and Ralph output can simply be thrown away and rerun from the same specs.
cards.landing: Cap autonomous PR size; the review burden is the limit

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you leave it going too long it will come up with more stuff to do
cards.claim: Ralph can be over-baked: left running past the point of done, the model invents extra work (for example post-quantum cryptography in a toy language), analogous to rolling back an overfit model to a checkpoint.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributes the cases to Geoff Huntley's experience and his own six-hour run
cards.landing: Bound loops by max iterations and a completion check

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Ralph is probably not the right final answer for how we build production software.
cards.claim: Ralph is valuable mainly as a lesson in how context windows work; engineers should learn the theory rather than just install the plugin; a chained spec-to-spec-to-code Ralph pipeline he tried did not produce a product he liked.
cards.evidence_detail: One failed experiment with chained Ralph loops
cards.landing: Do not adopt autonomous loops as production practice; take the context lesson

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: run it on a cron every night and only run three iterations of the loop
cards.claim: His production-safe version of Ralph is a nightly cron or GitHub Action running three iterations against a spec of the desired architecture, producing small incremental PRs he need not merge.
cards.evidence_detail: Used on an internal repo; no outcome numbers
cards.landing: Scheduled low-iteration improvement run; relates to the harness's scheduler and workflow ideas

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it is technically untrusted input
cards.claim: Never feed community-submitted issues to an agent running with skipped permissions; his team's Linear queue route requires a human to check for hidden prompts in HTML or markdown comments before the model sees anything.
cards.landing: Prompt-injection screening before any ticket text reaches an agent

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the hardest software problems in the world are not going to be done completely autonomously
cards.claim: For hard problems, work stays human-in-the-loop; the CodeLayer plan prompt uses a parent agent that runs each task in a sub-agent, checks the work, commits and moves to the next phase.
cards.landing: Parent-checks-sub-agent pattern in workflows

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models are not good at planning work in the way that, like, a human would
cards.claim: Models default to horizontal phases (move 40 things, then wire the endpoint, then refactor the front end); a human would move one thing end to end first, learn, and then continue, so plans need steering toward that.
cards.evidence_detail: One example with 40 front-end items moving to an API
cards.landing: Plan review checklist: phases must be vertical slices that surface surprises early

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: your instincts as an engineer are still really really good
cards.claim: Size plan tasks by how much code you would write by hand before running the app or tests; engineering instincts and old books (tracer bullets, from The Pragmatic Programmer) still apply when programming in English.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience-based; Matt Pocock supplied the tracer-bullet name, Dex agreed
cards.landing: Vertical-slice rule for plans; matches the repo's vertical-slice layout

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a learning test is... for verifying how an external library behaves
cards.claim: Write 'learning tests' that assert the real contract of an external system (his example is the closed-source Claude Agent SDK) before building on it; rerun them when behaviour seems to change, as when session-ID behaviour changed.
cards.evidence_detail: Session-ID contract change caught by rerunning a learning test three months later
cards.landing: Contract tests for external services (Meta WhatsApp API, R2, FCM) kept outside the default test run

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'd rather check every 100 200 lines of code
cards.claim: Size phases to a verifiable chunk, checking in every 100-200 lines on hard work, because a 2,000-line result that is broken gives you no way to know how to change the prompt.
cards.evidence_detail: Numbers 100-200 and 2,000 lines are his illustration
cards.landing: Review cadence and per-phase size cap

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: dual purpose plans
cards.claim: Write plans that work both ways: fire-and-forget through all phases, or check in after every phase when the work is delicate; and the key new skill is knowing how the model will know its output matches human intent.
cards.landing: Plan format with phase-level verification criteria

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: two to three X faster on most things
cards.claim: His target for brownfield codebases is a 2-3x speed-up for staff and principal engineers, plus standardisation across a team, because many engineers each using AI differently produces chaos even if each is fast.
cards.landing: Shared team workflow and skills library rather than individual styles

cards.source_title: Matt Pocock livestream: Chat with AI Coding Wizard Dex Horthy
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: rebuilt the entire product from scratch
cards.claim: In six weeks he rebuilt CodeLayer from scratch around more guided workflows after rolling it out to customers.
cards.landing: Context for CodeLayer as a source of workflow patterns

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you really don't want to run two clods in the same repo at the same time
cards.claim: Two agents in one checkout step on each other (for example contending on the Cargo lock, slowing both builds), so parallel agents need separate working directories.
cards.evidence_detail: Rust Cargo lock example from his own codebase
cards.landing: Parallel Workflow agents should use separate worktrees

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you will fail using GitWorkTree. That's my experience.
cards.claim: A worktree is only usable if one setup script (for example make setup) installs dependencies and copies untracked files such as .env and .claude; the repo defines setup, a generic create-worktree script runs it, and a failed setup auto-cleans the worktree.
cards.landing: Create-worktree script with setup and cleanup for the harness; this repo's .claude worktrees

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: copy the whole cloud directory
cards.claim: On creating a worktree, copy the git-ignored settings.local.json (personal permissions) by copying the whole .claude directory, since only committed files arrive in a new worktree.
cards.landing: Worktree bootstrap must carry local settings

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: by max is usually two
cards.claim: He rarely runs many agents at once (his maximum is usually two) and warns against over-parallelising because progress drops; worktrees are mostly a way to park work in a ready directory and resume tomorrow.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal usage, no numbers beyond two
cards.landing: Cap parallel agents; do not design for fan-out of six

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If you don't need this, you probably shouldn't use it.
cards.claim: Worktrees are not mandatory; he uses them because he keeps editing prompts and workflows on main while agents work elsewhere, calling it git stash on steroids.
cards.landing: Adopt worktrees only where parallel work exists

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the more you automate and the less you look into it the more likely it might deviate
cards.claim: A merge-watcher agent looping every 60 seconds can merge worker branches (with pre-commit tests mandatory in agent-only worktrees), but more automation means more deviation; his multi-claude manager-agent tool predates sub-agents and he warns not to over-parallelise.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo, translating a repo's server and client in parallel
cards.landing: Mandatory test pre-commit hook only inside agent worktrees; merge-gate by a watcher

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can actually prompt Claude to monitor the terminal of another Claude session
cards.claim: tmux lets one Claude list panes and capture the screen of another agent's terminal, so a manager agent can monitor workers.
cards.landing: Outside-observer check of agent state, relevant to self-reported compliance

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you cannot have the same branch checked out in two directories
cards.claim: A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time, which forces a structured one-branch-one-directory layout.
cards.landing: Worktree-per-branch convention

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Spend five minutes thinking about how you want to organize it
cards.claim: Fix a worktree convention up front (all under ~/worktree/repo/branch) and name branches person/feature (sometimes with a date); worktrees should be cleaned up after merge like local branches.
cards.landing: Naming and cleanup convention for harness worktrees

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we're really targeting developers who already know how Git works
cards.claim: He has not added worktree support to CodeLayer because the target users already know Git, and UIs that hide worktrees (Vibe Kanban, Conductor, Claude desktop) are worth trying for their opinions.
cards.evidence_detail: Product prioritisation statement; note HumanLayer release 0.201.0 later added worktrees (inventory line 62), a change of position
cards.landing: Dated position: later reversed in the product

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I literally just stage everything... then I let it go rip again
cards.claim: Review workflow: stage everything at each good checkpoint so the diff view shows only what the agent changed since the last reviewed state, keeping the risk within 10% of recoverable.
cards.evidence_detail: The statement is attributed by content to Vaibhav, the co-host, speaking about his own workflow; Dex may not own it
cards.landing: Checkpoint-staging review habit

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: give yourself a time-bounded bet
cards.claim: Adopt a new practice as a two-week time-bounded experiment, then re-evaluate; the worst case is perhaps 20-30% slower for two weeks.
cards.landing: Time-boxed trial framing, like the P1 cold-resume trial

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the more standardized you can make your process, the easier it is
cards.claim: A standard research-plan-implement workflow makes parallel agents comparable, because every checkpoint artifact has the same shape (three research docs look alike) so check-ins do not require rebuilding context.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued by analogy to standardised interviews
cards.landing: Uniform phase artifacts and closing message for fast re-entry

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: don't try to create work trees for each step of the workflow
cards.claim: Do research and planning on main, keep the markdown docs outside the code worktree (separate repo or vault, not merge-sensitive) and create the worktree only once the plan is good; overusing worktrees creates chaos.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer practice; people who make worktrees for research later need to merge only the documents
cards.landing: Plan files belong outside the implementation worktree; the draft-PR plan-first routine

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you want something more like Google Docs where it's like there's only one state
cards.claim: For shared design docs, plain git markdown forces pull/push sync and cannot be commented; he wants something between git and Google Docs that is live, version-viewable and agent-accessible (from a talk with Jeff Huber).
cards.landing: Plan-document storage and the knowledge-store design

cards.source_title: AI That Works: Git Worktrees for AI Coding Agents
cards.author: other
cards.quote: I actually just run the same thing on like five different models
cards.claim: Co-host Vaibhav runs the same task on several models in separate worktrees and merges the best pieces, finding design work benefits since no single model gets it right; Dex responds with parallel markdown drafts in different styles (not Dex's own idea).
cards.landing: Best-of-N for subjective output, if ever

gaps: Both are machine transcripts with no speaker labels, so attribution of some worktrees-episode passages between Dex and Vaibhav (the staging workflow, five-model runs, the BEP demo) is by content and uncertain.
The livestream ends early at 43 minutes when Matt had to leave, so the verifiability question Dex was answering is unfinished.
No numbers on effort levels, hooks, CLAUDE.md length or compliance appear in either source.
I did not find an exact inventory entry for the worktrees episode in a case-insensitive search for 'worktrees'; in_inventory false for those cards should be re-verified.

new_sources.title: HumanLayer create-worktree script and multi-claude tool (open source)
new_sources.why: Dex says the create-worktree script (copies .claude, runs make setup, cleans up on failure) and the May multi-claude manager-agent personas are open source; they are concrete worktree setup patterns.

new_sources.title: Geoff Huntley Ralph / cursed-lang repo
new_sources.why: Dex points to it as the long-running Ralph example showing emergent behaviour such as stray markdown files.
